extracted.intended_audience: education researchers, curriculum designers, and K-8 teachers concerned with reading comprehension, metacognition, and transfer to math/science instruction
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for diagnosing everyday versus academic thinking biases and teaching intentional comprehension-monitoring strategies (reciprocal teaching) to improve learning, with discussion of extending these methods to math and science. Emphasis on task analysis, scaffolding, and measuring instructional outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish everyday and academic thinking skills
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat the distinction between everyday and academic thinking skills as a heuristic: everyday thinking is effortless, scripted, and automatic; academic thinking emphasizes precision, deliberate evaluation, accurate understanding, and predictions consistent with provided facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that overreliance on everyday thinking skills in academic domains will cause students difficulty in solving intellectual problems. Instruction should make the distinction explicit and help students adopt more deliberate processing where required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foster intentional cognition rather than incidental learning
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective learning requires intentional, effortful cognition rather than passive reliance on incidental learning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage judicious allocation of effort: when reading to remember or to resolve difficulties learners must slow down and call into play comprehension-fostering operations. Anti-patterns: passive 'one-shot read', hoping understanding will occur automatically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comprehension-monitoring (split mental focus)
rubrics_metrics.description: Students must focus both on the material to be learned and simultaneously monitor their understanding and retention of it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach students to set acceptable comprehension criteria and to check whether those criteria are met. Use concrete checks (e.g., verbatim recall thresholds) before expecting abstract gist-monitoring. Emphasize planning, on-line checks, and corrective fix-up strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach self-regulatory activities for studying
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective readers deploy self-regulatory activities such as planning ahead, checking one's understanding, evaluating cost-effectiveness of strategies, and correcting comprehension or retention failures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Train students to choose strategies flexibly according to task demands (reading for gist vs. reading to remember vs. resolving comprehension problems). Model and practice these activities rather than assuming spontaneous use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use summarizing, questioning, clarifying, and predicting as core strategies
rubrics_metrics.description: Four strategies used by expert readers — summarizing, questioning, clarifying, and predicting — are both comprehension-fostering and comprehension-monitoring activities if used properly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instruct students explicitly in producing adequate synopses (paraphrase), generating likely test/teacher questions, identifying confusing passages for clarification, and making evidence-based predictions. Failure to perform these signals need for remedial action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid passive or superficial study heuristics (anti-patterns)
rubrics_metrics.description: Common ineffective student strategies include 'stare and hope', 'read twice if told to study', 'read the first line of every paragraph', and similar rote or minimal-effort tactics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diagnose these behaviors as insufficient for intentional comprehension; replace them with overtly taught strategies and scaffolded practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reciprocal teaching: dialogic, turn-taking instruction
rubrics_metrics.description: Reciprocal teaching has teacher and student take turns leading a dialogue on text segments: summarize content, ask questions a teacher/test might ask, discuss/clarify difficulties, and make predictions about future content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Embed activities in natural dialogue with feedback. Use assigned segments, alternate roles, and require overt performance of the four core strategies. This models expert tutoring and supports gradual student takeover of cognitive tasks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proleptic teaching / expert scaffolding
rubrics_metrics.description: Use proleptic teaching where novices participate before they can perform unaided; the expert initially models, explains, diagnoses, gives feedback, and gradually increases demands and fades support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expert scaffolding components: (a) model appropriate comprehension activities, (b) make covert strategies overt, (c) perform on-line diagnosis and monitoring, (d) give feedback and gently expand challenge. Novice roles: participate at current level, make competence overt, receive feedback, and progress incrementally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instructional design: task analysis and diagnosis of biases
rubrics_metrics.description: Design interventions by analyzing task components, diagnosing students' entering biases ('bugs'), and mapping steps from entering competence to desired competence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create scripts that make desired procedures simple, concrete, explicit, and easily modeled. Identify which existing student strategies are helpful or misleading and target those in instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address intuitive concepts and reasoning biases explicitly
rubrics_metrics.description: Many intuitive concepts (e.g., naive theories, misapplied heuristics about probability) are strongly held and can block acquisition of formal scientific concepts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instruction should make naive beliefs explicit and compare them with formal theory; present counterexamples and guided contrasts so students can confront and revise their intuitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagnose and remediate procedural 'bugs' in math and science
rubrics_metrics.description: For arithmetic and other procedural domains, identify systematic errors (bugs) and design instruction to help children reflect on the purpose and meaning of procedures rather than only drill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the same cycle: task analysis, diagnosis of misconceptions, scripted scaffolding, and opportunities for reflection. Use story-based problem contexts (e.g., 'Real Math Thinking' stories) and dialogues to surface and correct everyday-thinking biases that impede deductive reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expect and measure multiple outcomes when evaluating interventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Successful interventions should be evaluated on a range of outcomes including strategy use, role-taking, standardized and criterion comprehension scores, durability, transfer/generalization, and feasibility in natural settings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Palincsar & Brown reported ten measurable outcomes (examples): (1) improved ability to paraphrase/question/clarify/predict; (2) students move from passive observers to active teachers; (3) large quantitative gains on comprehension tests; (4) durable effects (weeks to months); (5) generalization to classroom; (6) transfer to different lab tasks; (7) standardized scores improved; (8) full reciprocal teaching outperforms direct-strategy instruction; (9) feasible for regular teachers; (10) teacher enthusiasm. Use these as criteria when assessing programs.

rubrics_metrics.name: General instructional aim: promote critical thinking over inert knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Instruction should promote critical thinking, evaluation, reflection, and application of principles rather than rote retention of inert knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foster activities akin to 'Socratic dialogues with themselves' — questioning, testing generalizations with counterexamples, extracting/applying principles, detecting tautologies and inconsistencies. Structure learning goals so knowledge is organized by hierarchy/taxonomy rather than only scripts or episodic themes.
